title: Reflexes, instincts and imprinting: what animals can do without lessons

summary.text: A gosling who hatches beside a man will follow that man, and not her own mother. She was born knowing how to follow, but not knowing whom. Animals, including humans, are born with reflexes, fixed patterns of movement and instincts. Each one waits for a trigger, and the trigger is often very simple. Your child tests what cold water on the face does to their heartbeat. They also test which drawn face people find cuter. They learn how a duckling fixes on a parent on the first day of life.
summary.art: A man walking across a meadow with a line of six grey goslings close behind his boots, and an adult goose standing alone in the distance.

intro.hook: A goose is rolling a stray egg back to her nest with her beak. A scientist takes the egg away halfway. The goose goes on with the rolling movement, all the way to the nest, with no egg under her beak. Why did she not stop?
intro.text: The goose was born able to make this rolling movement. A round thing lying near her nest sets the movement off. Once the movement starts, it runs to the end. Your body has patterns like this too. A blink, a swallow and a yawn each wait for a trigger. In this unit you find the triggers for three of your own reflexes. You test whether cold water on your face changes your heartbeat. You also meet the ducklings who follow the first moving thing they see.
intro.art: A grey goose on a nest of reeds stretching her neck out and drawing her beak back towards her feet, with a single egg lying apart on the grass and a hand lifting it away.

outcomes: I can say what a reflex is, and name the stimulus and the response of three reflexes.
I can explain what a fixed action pattern is, and give two examples.
I can explain what an instinct is, and how it differs from something learned.
I can explain what a sign stimulus is, and why a dummy can set off a behaviour.
I can test fairly what sets off the diving reflex, and say what my results show.
I can explain imprinting and the sensitive period, and tell how Konrad Lorenz tested them.
I can explain why a made-up trigger can work better than the real one.
I can give reasons why inborn behaviour and learning work together.

terms.meaning: The science of how animals behave, studied by watching them and testing them.
terms.example: Konrad Lorenz and Niko Tinbergen were ethologists. They watched geese, gulls and fish for years.
terms.art: A woman sitting still in tall grass with a notebook and binoculars, watching a goose and her goslings.

terms.meaning: Present from birth or hatching, without being taught. Another word for it is inborn.
terms.example: A duckling's urge to follow is innate. Nobody teaches it.
terms.art: A duckling stepping out of a broken eggshell and already looking around.

terms.meaning: The thing that sets off a response. In this unit we also call it the trigger.
terms.example: A drop of lemon juice on your tongue is a stimulus. It makes your mouth water.
terms.art: A drop of juice falling from a lemon wedge onto a child's tongue.

terms.meaning: What the body or the animal does after the stimulus.
terms.example: When something flies at your eye, the blink is the response.
terms.art: A child's face with both eyes shut tight as a small soft ball flies towards a clear sheet in front of her.

terms.meaning: A fast, automatic response of the body to one particular stimulus. Nobody has to learn it.
terms.example: Your hand pulls away from a hot tumbler before you feel the pain.
terms.art: A hand jerking back from a steaming steel tumbler on a kitchen counter.

terms.meaning: The slowing of the heart when the face is in cold water and the breath is held.
terms.example: A seal's heart slows as soon as she dives. Yours slows a little too.
terms.art: A seal swimming down under water, with a small heart drawn beside her and widely spaced beat marks.

terms.meaning: A set of movements that an animal is born able to do. The movements come in the same order each time and usually run to the end.
terms.example: A goose rolls an egg back to her nest in the same way every time.
terms.art: Three small drawings in a row of a goose reaching out, hooking an egg under her beak and drawing it back between her feet.

terms.meaning: A whole behaviour that an animal can carry out without being taught.
terms.example: A cuckoo chick pushes the other eggs out of the nest a day or so after hatching.
terms.art: A tiny featherless chick in a small nest heaving an egg over the edge with their back.

terms.meaning: The one feature of a thing that sets off an inborn behaviour.
terms.example: The red spot on a gull's beak is a sign stimulus. The chick pecks at the spot.
terms.art: A fluffy gull chick pecking at a red spot near the tip of a parent's yellow beak.

terms.meaning: A simple model that a scientist shows to an animal, to find out which feature the animal responds to.
terms.example: A cardboard gull head with a red spot is a dummy.
terms.art: A hand holding a flat cardboard gull head on a stick in front of a gull chick.

terms.meaning: A made-up trigger that works better than the real one, because the key feature is bigger or stronger.
terms.example: An oystercatcher chooses a giant plaster egg over her own egg.
terms.art: A black and white shore bird trying to sit on an egg almost as big as herself, with her own small speckled egg beside it.

terms.meaning: Fast learning that happens in a short time early in life and is very hard to undo. A young bird learns whom to follow.
terms.example: Goslings who first saw Konrad Lorenz followed him everywhere.
terms.art: A line of goslings swimming behind a man whose head and shoulders show above the water of a pond.

terms.meaning: The short time when a particular kind of learning, such as imprinting, can happen.
terms.example: For a mallard duckling, the sensitive period for imprinting is about the first day after hatching.
terms.art: A clock face beside a duckling, with the first part of the day shaded in a bright colour.

explanations.concept: A reflex is a fast response to one trigger
explanations.definition: A reflex is a fast, automatic response of the body to one particular stimulus. Nobody has to learn it.
explanations.description: Something rushes at your eye, and your eyelid shuts. You did not plan to shut it. The thing that sets a reflex off is called the stimulus, or the trigger. What the body then does is called the response. Each reflex has a trigger of its own. A drop of lemon juice makes your mouth water, but a loud clap does not. A reflex works in four steps. Sensors in the skin, the eye or the tongue pick up the trigger. A message runs along a nerve to the spinal cord or to the lowest part of the brain. A second message runs straight back to a muscle. The muscle pulls. The message does not wait for the parts of the brain that plan. That is why a reflex is so fast. When you touch a hot tumbler, your hand is already moving away before you feel the pain. After a tap below the kneecap, the thigh muscle starts to pull in less than a twentieth of a second. A nerve message is a tiny wave of electricity. It is made by charged particles moving in and out of the nerve cell. The fastest nerves carry a message about 100 metres in one second.
examples: The blink. When something rushes at the eye, the eyelid shuts.
Mouth-watering. When sour juice touches the tongue, saliva flows.
Pulling away. When skin touches something hot, the arm muscles pull the hand back.
The knee kick. After a tap below the kneecap, the lower leg swings forward.
explanations.art: A drawing of a child's arm touching a hot tumbler, with one arrow running from the fingertip up the arm to the spinal cord and a second arrow running back down to the arm muscle.

explanations.concept: The diving reflex: a reflex you share with seals
explanations.definition: In the diving reflex, the heart slows when the face is in cold water and the breath is held.
explanations.description: Cold water on the skin around your eyes and nose is picked up by a nerve of the face. If you are also holding your breath, a message goes to your heart, and your heart beats more slowly. Blood vessels in your arms and legs become narrower as well. Less blood goes to the limbs, and more is kept for the brain and the heart. In this way the oxygen from one breath lasts longer. In humans the heart usually slows by a tenth to a quarter. In a seal the change is far bigger. A seal's heart can drop from about 100 beats a minute to about 10 during a dive. Ducks, dolphins, otters and whales have the same reflex. So do newborn human babies. Scientists think the reflex is very old, and that all these animals inherited it from shared ancestors. The women divers of Jeju island in Korea, called haenyeo, depend on it every working day. They dive for shellfish on one breath. Chank shell divers have long done the same off Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu.
examples: A seal's heart slows from about 100 beats a minute to about 10 on a dive.
A human's heart slows by a tenth to a quarter with the face in cold water.
A duck's heart slows when she puts her head under water.
explanations.art: A split drawing: on the left a child with her face in a bowl of water, on the right a seal diving, each with a small heart and slow beat marks beside them.

explanations.concept: Fixed action patterns: movements that run to the end
explanations.definition: A fixed action pattern is a set of movements that an animal is born able to do. The movements come in the same order every time, and once started they usually run to the end.
explanations.description: A greylag goose sees an egg lying outside her nest. She stretches her neck, hooks the egg under her beak and rolls the egg back between her feet. In 1938 Konrad Lorenz and Niko Tinbergen took the egg away halfway through. The goose carried on. She drew her beak all the way back to the nest with nothing under it. Every greylag goose rolls an egg in this way, including geese who have never seen this done. That is a fixed action pattern. Your swallow is one too. Once food touches the back of your mouth, more than 20 muscles work in a set order. You cannot stop them halfway. A yawn is another. In Germany, the scientist Irenäus Eibl-Eibesfeldt raised red squirrels alone, with no soil and no nuts. Later he gave each squirrel a nut on a bare floor. The squirrels scraped at the floor, pressed the nut down with their noses and made covering movements over it. A fixed pattern is useful because it works the very first time, with no practice. Scientists today often say 'modal action pattern', because no two runs are exactly alike. A goose steers the egg from side to side when the egg wobbles. So part of the pattern is fixed, and part is adjusted as she goes.
examples: A goose rolling an egg back to her nest.
A person swallowing a mouthful of water.
A yawn, which lasts about six seconds and is hard to stop once begun.
A squirrel making digging and covering movements over a nut.
explanations.art: A red squirrel on a bare wooden floor pressing a nut down with their nose, with scratch marks drawn on the floor beside the nut.

explanations.concept: Instincts: whole behaviours that need no teacher
explanations.definition: An instinct is a whole behaviour that an animal can carry out without being taught. It is inherited from the parents, as the shape of a beak is.
explanations.description: A common cuckoo chick hatches in the nest of another kind of bird. On the first or second day, the chick is still blind and has no feathers. The chick heaves the other eggs over the edge with their back. The chick has never seen this done. A koel is raised by crows and hears cawing all day. The young koel still grows up to call 'ku-oo' like a koel. A duckling raised by a hen walks into water and swims. These are instincts. An instinct is usually built from several fixed patterns, with steering from the senses and choices along the way. A bird building her first nest uses inborn movements. She also chooses the branch, tests each twig and gets better with every nest. So an instinct gives an animal a strong start, and learning improves on that start. Instinct matters most for things that must go right the first time, with no teacher near. Most insects and spiders never meet their parents, so they depend on instinct for much of what they do. They learn as well. Elephants, crows and humans grow up slowly beside their elders, and learn much more of what they do. They have instincts too.
examples: A cuckoo chick pushing eggs out of the nest.
A koel raised by crows calling like a koel.
A duckling raised by a hen swimming on the first try.
A newborn calf standing up and searching for the udder.
explanations.art: A grey-brown koel fledgling sitting in a crow's nest of sticks with a house crow perched beside them, and a small 'ku-oo' written near the koel's open beak.

explanations.concept: Sign stimuli: one small feature sets off the behaviour
explanations.definition: A sign stimulus is the one feature of a thing that sets off an inborn behaviour. Scientists find it by showing animals simple models called dummies.
explanations.description: A herring gull has a red spot on the lower part of her yellow beak. Her chick pecks at the spot, and the pecking makes her bring up food. Niko Tinbergen and his student Ab Perdeck showed gull chicks cardboard heads. A head with no spot got few pecks. A head with a red spot got many. The chick was responding mostly to one feature, a red patch on a long thin shape. A male stickleback fish guards his nest in spring, when other males have red undersides. Tinbergen reported that males attacked rough wax lumps with red undersides. They left lifelike models with no red alone. A mother hen runs to a chick she can hear cheeping, even behind a screen. In one old test, a hen could see a chick struggling under a glass cover but could not hear them. She did not go to the chick. A simple trigger is quick to pick up, and in nature it is nearly always right. In a gull colony, a red spot above a chick really is a parent. But a simple trigger can be fooled. In Australia, male jewel beetles were found clinging to brown beer bottles beside the road. The shiny brown glass with its small bumps had the features of a female beetle's back.
examples: A gull chick pecks at the red spot on a parent's beak.
A male stickleback attacks anything with a red underside.
A mother hen comes running when she hears a chick cheeping.
A goose rolls in any round thing that lies near her nest.
explanations.art: Three cardboard gull heads on sticks in a row: one plain yellow, one with a red spot, and one thin red stick with white bands, with a gull chick pecking at the stick.

explanations.concept: Supernormal stimuli: stronger than the real thing
explanations.definition: A supernormal stimulus is a made-up trigger that works better than the real one. Its key feature has been made bigger or stronger.
explanations.description: Tinbergen offered an oystercatcher, who is a shore bird, a choice of eggs to sit on. One was her own. One was a giant egg, far too big for her to cover. She tried to sit on the giant egg. Herring gull chicks were shown a lifelike model of a parent's head and a thin red stick with white bands. They pecked more at the stick. The stick had more of what the chicks respond to: redness, thinness and contrast. In nature this causes no trouble, because no real egg is ever that big. So a bird never needed an inborn rule that says an egg can be too big. Only a person with paint and plaster can make an egg bigger than any real one. Cuckoo chicks do something similar to their foster parents. The inside of a cuckoo chick's open mouth is bright orange-red. One cuckoo chick's begging call sounds like a whole nest of chicks. A small reed warbler goes on feeding a cuckoo chick who is several times her own size. People make supernormal stimuli for each other all the time. A sweet tastes sweeter than any fruit does. A cartoon animal has eyes bigger than any real baby's eyes.
examples: An oystercatcher choosing a giant egg.
Gull chicks pecking more at a striped red stick than at a model beak.
A reed warbler feeding a cuckoo chick much bigger than herself.
A sweet that is sweeter than a ripe mango.
explanations.art: A small brown reed warbler standing on the back of a huge cuckoo chick to drop an insect into the chick's wide orange mouth.

explanations.concept: Why do big eyes look cute? A possible trigger in humans
explanations.definition: The baby schema is a set of features that babies have: a large head, a high forehead, big eyes low on the face, round cheeks and a small nose and chin. In 1943 Konrad Lorenz proposed that these features set off caring in adults.
explanations.description: Human babies, puppies, kittens and chicks share these features. Lorenz's idea was that the features work as a sign stimulus for humans. An adult who sees them feels an urge to look after the small one. Tests support part of this. Scientists have changed photos of babies to make the eyes bigger and the face rounder. People rated the changed babies as cuter, and said they wanted to look after them more. Children as young as three respond in the same way. Toy makers and cartoon artists use this. Over fifty years, the artists who drew Mickey Mouse gave him a bigger head and bigger eyes. That is a supernormal stimulus made with a pencil. What is not settled is how much of the response is inborn. People also learn what counts as cute from the toys and cartoons around them. So this is an idea with some good evidence. You test part of the idea yourself in the Big Eyes Test.
examples: A puppy's round head and big eyes make many people say 'aww'.
Soft toys are made with bigger heads and eyes than real animals have.
Cartoon babies have foreheads much higher than real babies' foreheads.

perspectives.explanation: The response is inborn. Baby features are a sign stimulus that sets off caring in adults. A red spot sets off pecking in a gull chick in the same way.

perspectives.who: Scientists who doubt that it is all inborn
perspectives.explanation: People do respond to baby features. But children grow up surrounded by big-eyed toys and cartoons, so some of the response may be learned.

explanations.art: A real kitten and a soft toy kitten side by side, the toy with a much bigger head and eyes.

explanations.concept: Imprinting: a duckling learns whom to follow
explanations.definition: Imprinting is a fast kind of learning that happens during a short time early in life. A young bird learns whom to follow, and the learning is very hard to undo.
explanations.description: A greylag gosling can walk within a day of hatching. She is born with the urge to follow, and with the movements for following. But she is not born knowing what her mother looks like. In her first day she fixes on a large thing that moves near her and makes sounds. In nature that thing is her mother. Konrad Lorenz let goslings hatch in an incubator, so that the first moving thing they saw was Lorenz. They followed him across fields and into the river, and stayed away from adult geese. Mallard ducklings were harder to lead. They followed Lorenz only when he squatted low and quacked without stopping. The short time when imprinting can happen is called the sensitive period. In 1959 Eckhard Hess reported tests on mallard ducklings with a model duck that moved round a track. Ducklings imprinted most strongly at 13 to 16 hours old. After about 30 hours, hardly any did. Ducklings have also imprinted on moving boxes and balls. Imprinting is found mostly in birds who walk soon after hatching, such as ducks, geese and chickens. A sparrow chick stays in the nest, and the parents come to the chick. So the chick has no need to follow anyone. Other animals have their own kinds of imprinting. A ewe learns the smell of her lamb in the first hours after birth. Young salmon learn the smell of their home stream, and find the stream again years later. Human babies do not imprint as ducklings do. But a newborn baby already prefers their mother's voice, which they heard before birth.
examples: Goslings following the person who hatched them.
A mallard duckling following a model duck round a track.
A ewe who knows her own lamb by smell within hours.
A salmon returning to the stream where they hatched.
explanations.art: A man squatting low in a meadow and quacking, with a line of mallard ducklings hurrying after him and two surprised walkers looking over a fence.

explanations.concept: Where is an instinct kept? Genes build the wiring
explanations.definition: Scientists think that inborn behaviour comes from the way nerve cells are linked before birth. Genes guide this linking. The details are known for very few behaviours.
explanations.description: A gene is a stretch of DNA. DNA is the long molecule in every cell that is copied from parents to their young. Genes do not carry drawings of nests or burrows. They carry instructions for building a body, cell by cell, including the nerve cells and the links between them. A reflex is the simplest case. A sensor, a nerve going in, a nerve going out and a muscle are all linked before birth. Bigger behaviours are harder to trace. Hopi Hoekstra and her team studied two kinds of American mice. Oldfield mice dig a long burrow with an escape tunnel. Deer mice dig a short burrow with no escape tunnel. Mice raised in cages had never seen a burrow. They still dug the burrow of their own kind. In 2013 the team found three regions of DNA linked to the length of the tunnel. One more region was linked to the escape tunnel. This shows that a behaviour can be inherited in parts. Nobody can yet read a stretch of DNA and say which behaviour it will build. Imprinting leaves a trace as well. Gabriel Horn, Patrick Bateson and Steven Rose studied chicks. They found a small region of the brain that changes when a chick imprints.
examples: A reflex, in which a sensor, two nerves and a muscle are linked together before birth.
Oldfield mice raised in cages still dig a long burrow with an escape tunnel.
A small region of a chick's brain changes during imprinting.
explanations.art: A cut-away view of sandy ground showing a long mouse burrow with a nest chamber and a second tunnel rising almost to the surface, and a small mouse at the entrance.

explanations.definition: Scientists agree that some behaviours appear without any teaching. They disagree about whether 'inborn' and 'learned' can ever be fully separated.
explanations.description: A duckling just out of the egg turns towards the call of a mother duck of their own kind. That looks purely inborn. Gilbert Gottlieb tested it. Ducklings call softly inside the egg before hatching, and they hear themselves and their brothers and sisters. Gottlieb stopped some duck embryos from making or hearing these calls. After hatching, those ducklings no longer picked out the right mother's call. So even this instinct needed an experience, though nobody taught it.
examples: A duckling picks out the call of their own kind of mother.
A koel raised by crows calls like a koel.

perspectives.explanation: Instinct and learning are two separate things. An inborn pattern is inherited whole, as a bone is. Learning is added at set points, as in imprinting.

perspectives.who: Daniel Lehrman in 1953, and later Gilbert Gottlieb
perspectives.explanation: No behaviour is simply in the genes. Every behaviour grows step by step, as genes, body and surroundings act on each other, starting inside the egg. Calling it instinct hides the question of how it grows.
Both points are right. Some behaviours appear in every healthy animal of a kind, and 'innate' is a short name for those. Even they need the right surroundings while the body grows.

An animal acting by instinct is sensing, feeling and choosing the whole time. A goose who rolls an egg steers the egg, and she chose where to build her nest. Instinct is the starting point for her choices.

explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a duck egg with a duckling curled inside, their beak slightly open, and small sound marks inside the shell.

agreed.text: Reflexes are inborn and fast, and they run through the spinal cord or the lowest part of the brain.
agreed.evidence: Doctors find the same reflexes in every healthy newborn baby. The time between a tap on the knee and the pull of the thigh muscle has been measured many times.

agreed.text: Humans share the diving reflex with seals, ducks and other air-breathing animals.
agreed.evidence: Paul Bert measured the slowing heart in diving ducks in 1870. Per Scholander measured it in seals in 1940. It has been measured in people in many laboratories since.

agreed.text: Animals can carry out complicated behaviour that they have never seen.
agreed.evidence: Edward Jenner described the cuckoo chick pushing out eggs in 1788. Squirrels raised alone made burying movements. Mice raised in cages dug the burrow of their own kind.

agreed.text: Many inborn behaviours are set off by one simple feature, the sign stimulus.
agreed.evidence: Tinbergen and others showed dummies to gull chicks, sticklebacks and other animals. David Lack found that a European robin attacked a bunch of red feathers.

agreed.text: Young ducks, geese and chickens imprint during a short sensitive period after hatching.
agreed.evidence: Douglas Spalding reported it in chicks in 1873, Oskar Heinroth in goslings in 1911 and Konrad Lorenz in 1935. Eckhard Hess measured the timing in ducklings in 1959.

agreed.text: Inborn behaviour is inherited through DNA.
agreed.evidence: Hopi Hoekstra's team crossed two kinds of mice and linked parts of their burrow shape to particular regions of DNA.

challenging.claim: Douglas Spalding described imprinting sixty years before Konrad Lorenz.
challenging.who: Historians of science, and the biologist J. B. S. Haldane, who had Spalding's paper reprinted in 1954.
challenging.for: Spalding's paper of 1873 reports that chicks followed the first moving thing they saw. It also reports that this stopped working after a few days.
challenging.against: Lorenz gave imprinting its name, tested it in more ways and made the idea widely known. Both men deserve credit.

challenging.claim: A male stickleback attacks anything with a red underside.
challenging.who: Niko Tinbergen, from tests he reported in 1948 and 1951.
challenging.for: In his tests, males attacked rough models with red undersides and left lifelike models without red alone.
challenging.against: Later scientists repeated the tests with more fish. In 1985 William Rowland and Piet Sevenster found that many males did not attack red dummies more. Red matters, but less simply than Tinbergen said.

challenging.claim: A wasp acting by instinct will repeat the same steps for ever, whatever happens.
challenging.who: Many books, retelling a test by Jean-Henri Fabre on a digger wasp.
challenging.for: Fabre moved a wasp's cricket away from her burrow while she was inside checking it. She dragged it back and checked the burrow again, about forty times in a row.
challenging.against: Fabre himself wrote that wasps from another colony stopped after two or three tries and took the cricket straight in. In 2013 Fred Keijzer showed that later books left that part out.

challenging.claim: Imprinting happens in one moment and can never be changed.
challenging.who: Konrad Lorenz, in his early writing.
challenging.for: Birds raised by hand often stayed attached to people for life.
challenging.against: Eckhard Hess, Patrick Bateson and others found that imprinting builds up over hours. The sensitive period has soft edges, and a young bird can sometimes come to prefer a second thing.

challenging.claim: Humans have no instincts. Everything a person does is learned.
challenging.who: John B. Watson, an American psychologist, in the 1920s.
challenging.for: Humans learn far more than most animals, and people in different places live very differently.
challenging.against: Every newborn baby sucks, grasps, turns towards a touch on the cheek and looks longer at face-like patterns. William James argued in 1890 that humans have more instincts than other animals, not fewer.

big_questions.q: You never learned to slow your heart in cold water, yet your body knows how. Is that knowledge really yours, even though you did not learn it?
big_questions.hint: Think about other things you have that you did not make: your eyes, your name, your first language.

big_questions.q: A goose goes on with the rolling movement after the egg is gone. What might she be noticing while she does it?
big_questions.hint: Nobody can ask her. What could a scientist watch for, to find out?

big_questions.q: A gosling who follows a man is following her inborn rule exactly. The rule is to follow the first big moving thing she sees. So where did the mistake come from?
big_questions.hint: Her rule is 'follow the first big moving thing'. In nature that thing is always her mother.

big_questions.q: A cartoon can look cuter than a real baby. Can made-up things pull at us harder than real things?
big_questions.hint: Think about sweets and fruit, or a video game and a real game of catch.

big_questions.q: Which is the better start in life: to be born knowing a lot, or to be born able to learn a lot?
big_questions.hint: A wasp never meets her mother. An elephant calf stays beside hers for years.

big_questions.q: How much of what you did today did you plan, and how much did your body do without asking you?
big_questions.hint: Count the blinks, swallows, breaths and yawns that nobody planned.

story.title: The Blue Chappals
story.note: Ammu, Ammachi, Unni and the duckling Minnu are made up. These things are real. In Kuttanad in Kerala, herders walk large flocks of ducks through the paddy fields after the harvest. Duck eggs are often hatched under hens. A duckling follows the first moving thing she sees on her first day. Ducklings in tests have followed moving boxes and balls. Ducklings swim without being shown how. The pair of chappals is imagined, and fits these findings.
text: In Kuttanad, when the paddy has been cut, the fields belong to the ducks. Ammu's grandmother walked three hundred of them out every morning. She carried a long pole with a white cloth tied to the tip. Where the cloth went, the ducks went.

Ammu was nine, and she had come from Kochi for the Onam holidays. Her job was small. In the shed, a brown hen was sitting on the last twelve duck eggs. Ammu had to tell Ammachi when they began to crack.

Eleven cracked on a Tuesday night. By morning, eleven ducklings were peeping under the hen's wings. The twelfth egg had rolled to the edge of the nest. Ammu picked the egg up to throw away. Something inside tapped against her palm.
She put the egg in half a coconut shell lined with an old towel, and set the shell on the warm kitchen step. Then she sat down beside it and waited.
Near noon the shell split round the top, like a lid. A wet head pushed out. The duckling lay still for a long time, breathing. Then she lifted her head and looked about.
"Ammachi!" Ammu jumped up and ran to the shed. Her blue rubber chappals slapped on the stone. The duckling watched them go.
From that hour, the duckling went wherever Ammu went. She went to the well. She went to the gate. When Ammu sat down, the duckling sat on her foot. Ammu named her Minnu.
"Put her with the others," Ammachi said.
Ammu tucked Minnu under the hen, among the eleven. Minnu climbed out and ran back across the yard, crying. Ammu tried three times. Minnu came back three times.
"She saw you first," said Ammachi. "A duckling follows whatever she sees moving on her first day. After that, the door shuts. I once had one who followed a goat."
"So she thinks I am her mother?"
"I don't know what she thinks," said Ammachi. "I know what she does."
Ammu's cousin Unni, who was seven, thought it was wonderful. "She loves you," he said.

Ammu was not sure, and she had a worry. In nine days she would go home to a flat on the fourth floor. A duck could not live there. And a duck who would not stay with the flock would be alone in the fields, where the kites circled.
So she began to watch Minnu the way Ammachi watched ducks, without hurrying.

She noticed two things. One evening she sat on the veranda wall with her feet tucked up under her. Minnu ran about below, peeping loudly, though Ammu's face was right there above her. And when Ammu left her chappals at the kitchen door and went in barefoot, Minnu did not follow her in. Minnu sat down beside the chappals and went quiet.
Ammu thought about that all through dinner.
In the morning she called Unni. "Put on my chappals," she said. "Walk to the well. Don't look back."
"They're too big."
"That doesn't matter. Walk."

Unni shuffled off across the yard. Minnu got up and hurried after him, with her beak a finger's width behind the blue heels. Ammu walked the other way, barefoot, calling softly. Minnu did not turn her head.
"She doesn't know you at all!" Unni shouted from the well.
"She knows what she saw," Ammu said. She held her hand low, at the height of a duckling's eye. "From down here, what was moving? Not my face. These."
It stung a little, and she did not say so.
"Now watch," she told Unni. "We change one thing at a time. Take them off and carry them."
Unni carried the chappals in his hands, high up. Minnu stood still and cried. He put them on the ground and pulled them along with a string. Minnu followed the string.
"On her first day, the first things she saw were blue chappals moving along the ground," Ammu said. "So to her, that is what a mother looks like."

That afternoon Ammachi put on the blue chappals. They pinched, and she grumbled. She walked into the duckling pen and stood among the eleven and the hen. Minnu settled beside her heels. The eleven pressed in around Minnu, because ducklings like a warm heap. That night Minnu slept in the heap.
Every day after that, the chappals went into the pen, with Ammachi in them. Every day Minnu sat a little further from the blue heels and a little deeper among the eleven.

On the eighth day, Ammachi led the young ones down to the canal for the first time. The hen came too, and Minnu trotted behind the chappals. At the edge the eleven slid straight into the water and paddled off. Nobody had shown them how. The hen ran up and down the bank, clucking with alarm.
Minnu stopped beside the chappals. A ripple touched her feet. She dipped her beak. Then she was in the water as well, paddling hard after the others, with her tail wagging.
"There are no chappals in a canal," said Ammachi, and stepped out of them with a sigh.
Ammu went home to Kochi in new green chappals from the shop at the junction. The blue ones stayed in Kuttanad.

A month later Ammachi sent a message. "Your duck walks in the middle of the flock now. She follows the white cloth like the rest. But yesterday the fish seller came by in blue slippers, and she went halfway to the road after him."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Minnu had not fixed on Ammu as a person. She had fixed on the first thing she saw moving at the height of a duckling's eye. That was a pair of blue chappals. Ammu found this out by changing one thing at a time. That is how Lorenz and Hess studied imprinting.
ask: Why did Minnu follow Unni when he wore the blue chappals?
What did Ammu learn when Unni carried the chappals high in his hands?
Nobody showed the ducklings how to swim. What else can a duckling do without being shown?

A small boy shuffling across a yard in blue chappals that are too big for him, with a duckling close behind his heels and a barefoot girl walking the other way.
