games.title: Which One Did They Choose? Sixteen real tests
games.context: This is a card game about real tests that scientists did with animals. Each card describes a test, and you predict what the animal did.

setup.art: Sixteen cards in a shuffled pile on a table, face up, with a pencil and a score page beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. Shuffle them into a pile, fronts up.

setup.art: A girl reading the front of a card aloud while a woman holds up one finger to show her guess.
setup.caption: 2. Read the front. Everyone says a guess and a reason.

setup.art: The card turned over to show the back, and a tick being written on the score page.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Read what the animal really did.

printables.title: 16 test cards: a real test on the front, and what the animal did on the back

items.f: A male stickleback fish guards his nest. He is shown a lifelike model fish with no red, and a rough wax lump with a red underside. Which one does he attack?
items.b: The red wax lump. Niko Tinbergen reported this. A red underside is the trigger, because rival males are red below in spring.

items.f: A herring gull chick is shown two cardboard heads. One has a plain yellow beak. One has a red spot on the beak. Which one gets more pecks?
items.b: The one with the red spot. The red spot is the sign stimulus for pecking. Tinbergen and Perdeck, 1950.

items.f: A gull chick is shown a lifelike model of a parent's head. The chick is also shown a thin red stick with three white bands. Which one gets more pecks?
items.b: The red stick. It has more redness and contrast than a real beak. It is a supernormal stimulus.

items.f: A goose is rolling an egg back to her nest. The egg is taken away halfway. Does she stop, or finish the movement?
items.b: She finishes the movement with nothing under her beak. A fixed action pattern usually runs to the end. Lorenz and Tinbergen, 1938.

items.f: An oystercatcher is a shore bird. She can sit on her own egg, or on a giant egg far too big to cover. Which one does she choose?
items.b: The giant egg. Bigger is a stronger trigger for sitting. In nature no egg is ever that big.

items.f: A male European robin guards his garden. He is shown a stuffed young robin with a brown breast, and a bunch of red feathers on a wire. Which one does he attack?
items.b: The bunch of red feathers. David Lack found that the red breast is the trigger for attack.

items.f: A mother hen can see one chick struggling under a glass cover, but cannot hear them. She can hear another chick cheeping behind a screen. Which chick does she go to?
items.b: The chick she can hear. The cheeping sound is the trigger for her rescue, more than the sight of the chick.

items.f: Goslings hatch in an incubator, and the first moving thing they see is a man. Later they can follow him or an adult goose. Whom do they follow?
items.b: The man. Konrad Lorenz was that man. The goslings had imprinted on him.

items.f: One mallard duckling first sees a moving model duck at 15 hours old. Another first sees it at 35 hours old. Which duckling follows the model later?
items.b: The duckling who was 15 hours old. Eckhard Hess found that the sensitive period is nearly over by 30 hours.

items.f: A red squirrel is raised alone, with no soil and no nuts. Then the squirrel is given a nut on a bare wooden floor. What does the squirrel do?
items.b: The squirrel scrapes the floor, presses the nut down and makes covering movements. The burying pattern is inborn.

items.f: A common cuckoo chick hatches in a reed warbler's nest. The chick is one day old, blind and without feathers. What does the chick do to the other eggs?
items.b: The chick pushes them out of the nest with their back. Edward Jenner described this in 1788. Nobody shows the chick how.

items.f: In Australia, a male jewel beetle can go to a female beetle or to a brown beer bottle. Scientists found many males on one of these. Which one?
items.b: The bottle. The shiny brown glass with small bumps was a supernormal stimulus.

items.f: A newborn human baby is a few minutes old. The baby is shown a paddle with a simple drawn face. Then the baby is shown a paddle with the same parts jumbled. Which paddle does the baby follow further with their eyes?
items.b: The face. Newborn babies turn further to follow a face-like pattern. Humans are born with a pull towards faces.

items.f: Ducklings imprint on two shapes that are the same, such as two balls. Later they can follow two new shapes that match, or two that differ. Which pair do most follow?
items.b: The matching pair. In 2016 Antone Martinho and Alex Kacelnik showed that ducklings imprint on 'same' or 'different' as well as on shape.

items.f: Adults watch a five-minute film of people yawning. Other adults watch a film of people smiling. In which group do more people yawn?
items.b: The yawn group. In Robert Provine's test, about half of them yawned. Seeing a yawn is a trigger for a yawn.

items.f: A toad sees a small strip moving lengthwise, like a worm crawling. Then the toad sees the same strip turned upright and moving sideways. Which one does the toad snap at?
items.b: The strip moving lengthwise. Jörg-Peter Ewert found that the direction of movement is the trigger. The shape is the same.

printables.title: Score sheet: one row for each player

rules: Shuffle the 16 cards and put them in a pile with the fronts up.
One player reads the front of the top card aloud. Nobody looks at the back yet.
Every player, including the reader, says a guess and gives one reason for it.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. Each player with the right guess scores 1 point.
Take turns to be the reader. Play all 16 cards.
Playing alone? Read the front, say your guess and your reason aloud, then turn the card over.
The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, try to beat 10 out of 16.

flow.do: Cut out the 16 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile with the fronts up. Give each player a row on the score sheet.
flow.say: Every card describes a test that a scientist really did. The front asks what the animal chose. The back tells what happened.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Keep the fronts up.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which One Did They Choose. You set up the 16 test cards.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards by the rules. After each card, ask for the reason before you turn the card over.
flow.say: Say your guess and your reason. Then we turn the card over. A wrong guess with a good reason is still good thinking.
flow.kid: Read the card. Guess what the animal did. Say why.

good: The animal goes for the strongest feature.
The first thing a baby bird sees matters most.
A pattern keeps going once it starts.

flow.parent: Most children guess that the animal picks the lifelike model. Let the cards surprise them. Do not explain the pattern yet.
flow.context: In this step of Which One Did They Choose you play the first eight test cards.

flow.do: Play the last eight cards the same way. Keep the score.
flow.say: We will play eight more cards. Before each guess, ask yourself which one feature the animal might be responding to.
flow.kid: Play eight more cards. Look for the one feature that matters.
flow.context: In this step of Which One Did They Choose you play the last eight test cards.

flow.do: Count the points. Then spread out all 16 cards with the backs up. Ask your child to find three cards where a dummy beat the real thing.
flow.say: Find three cards where the animal chose a dummy over the real thing. What did each dummy have more of?
flow.kid: Find three cards where a dummy won. What did the dummy have more of?

check.q: A gull chick pecks more at a striped red stick than at a model of a real beak. Why?
options: The stick has more of the feature that sets off pecking
The stick tastes of fish
The chick knows the stick is a toy
check.why: The chick responds to redness and contrast on a thin shape. The stick has more of these than a real beak, so it sets off more pecks. If you chose the taste of fish, remember that the chick pecks before tasting anything.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which One Did They Choose. You look for cards where a dummy beat the real thing.

games.title: Crack the Trigger: the dummy game
games.context: This is a guessing game for two or more players. One player is an animal with a secret trigger. The other player is a scientist who shows dummies, one at a time, to find the trigger.

setup.art: Sixteen small cards laid out in four rows on a table, each with four words written on it, such as 'Red, round, moving, silent'.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the 16 dummy cards, face up.

setup.art: A child holding one card close to her chest and smiling, while a woman opposite holds up a dummy card.
setup.caption: 2. The animal player takes one secret trigger card. The scientist shows a dummy.

setup.art: Two piles of dummy cards on the table, one under a slip of paper marked 'Respond' and one under a slip marked 'Ignore'.
setup.caption: 3. The animal says 'respond' or 'ignore'. Sort the dummies into two piles.

printables.title: 6 secret trigger cards
items: Stickleback father guarding his nest. You respond to every dummy that is RED. You ignore all others.
Goose on her nest. You respond to every dummy that is ROUND. You ignore all others.
Duckling on your first day. You respond to every dummy that is MOVING. You ignore all others.
Mother hen. You respond to every dummy that is CHEEPING. You ignore all others.
Gull chick. You respond only to dummies that are both RED and LONG. You ignore all others.
Toad. You respond only to dummies that are both LONG and MOVING. You ignore all others.

rules: Lay the 16 dummy cards face up. Each dummy has a colour, a shape, a movement and a sound.
One player is the animal. The animal takes one trigger card, reads the card silently and keeps the card hidden.
The other player is the scientist. The scientist picks any dummy card and holds it up.
The animal says 'respond' or 'ignore', and must follow the trigger card exactly.
The scientist puts the dummy on the Respond pile or the Ignore pile, and then shows another dummy.
At any time the scientist may name the trigger. A right answer scores 10 points, minus 1 for every dummy shown.
A wrong answer costs 2 points, and the round goes on.
Swap roles after each round. With three or more players, the scientists work as a team.
After four rounds, the player or team with the most points wins. The six trigger cards are simple forms of real findings.

flow.do: Cut out the 6 trigger cards and the 16 dummy cards. Lay the dummy cards face up. Shuffle the trigger cards face down. Read the rules together.
flow.say: Scientists cannot ask a goose what sets off her egg rolling. They show her dummies and watch. In this game you do the same.
flow.kid: Lay out the dummy cards. Shuffle the trigger cards face down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Crack the Trigger. You set out the dummy cards and the secret trigger cards.

flow.do: Play four rounds by the rules, and swap roles each time. Write down the score after each round.
flow.say: Show me one dummy at a time. I will say 'respond' or 'ignore'. Name my trigger when you are sure.
flow.kid: Show one dummy. Hear 'respond' or 'ignore'. Then name the trigger.
flow.parent: If your child is stuck, suggest this. Find one dummy that gets a response. Then show a dummy that differs from it in one feature only. If the trigger is a single feature, five dummies are enough to find it. Show one dummy, then change one feature at a time.

ask.q: Which dummy will you show next, and why that one?
good: One that changes only the colour.
I change one feature and keep the rest the same.
I need to know if the sound matters.

flow.context: In this step of Crack the Trigger you play four rounds and try to find each secret trigger.

flow.do: Look at the scores. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Which rounds took the fewest dummies? What did you do differently in those rounds?
flow.kid: Which round was quickest? What did you do in that round?

check.q: A red, round, moving, silent dummy gets a response. Which dummy should a scientist show next?
options: A grey, round, moving, silent dummy
A grey, long, still, cheeping dummy
The same dummy again
check.why: The grey, round, moving, silent dummy changes only the colour. If the animal now ignores this dummy, colour is part of the trigger. If you chose the dummy that changes everything, a different answer would not tell you which feature mattered.

flow.context: This is the last step of Crack the Trigger. You talk about how to find a trigger with the fewest dummies.

experiments.title: The Cold Face Test: what does cold water on your face do to your heartbeat?
experiments.question: When you hold your breath with your face in cold water, does your heart beat faster, slower or the same? Does cold water on your hand do the same thing?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. With your face in cold water and your breath held, will your heart beat faster, slower or the same? Will a cold hand do the same thing as a cold face? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Sit on the same chair for every try, and rest for one minute before each try. Hold your breath for 20 seconds every time, after a normal breath in. The grown-up counts the pulse for the same 15 seconds every time, from second 5 to second 20. Change only one thing between the tests: nothing wet, the hand in the water, or the face in the water. Do each test three times, because one count can be wrong by a beat or two.
results_table: Pulse count in 15 seconds: try 1, try 2 and try 3
The middle count of the three

materials.item: a wide bowl or a small tub, at least 25 centimetres across, filled with water 10 centimetres deep
a tray of ice cubes, or 1 litre of cold water from the fridge
a towel
a phone timer or a clock that shows seconds
a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays beside the child for the whole test. The child holds their breath for 20 seconds at most and may lift their face at any moment. Use cold water, not painfully cold water. Leave this test out if your child has a cold, an ear infection, breathing trouble or any heart condition.
experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows: resting, breath held, breath held with a hand in cold water, and breath held with the face in cold water. Write three pulse counts in each row. Then circle the middle count of each three.
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up counts your pulse while you hold your breath in three ways: with nothing wet, with a hand in cold water and with your face in cold water. You find out what sets off the diving reflex.

setup.art: A grown-up sitting beside a child at a table with two fingers resting on the inside of the child's wrist, and a phone showing a timer.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up finds your pulse and counts it for 15 seconds.

setup.art: The child sitting upright with cheeks slightly puffed, holding her breath, while the grown-up counts her pulse.
setup.caption: 2. Hold your breath for 20 seconds with nothing wet. The grown-up counts again.

setup.art: The child holding her breath with one hand in a wide bowl of water with ice cubes floating in it, while the grown-up holds her other wrist.
setup.caption: 3. Hold your breath with one hand in the cold water.

setup.art: The child leaning over the bowl with her forehead, eyes and nose under the water, while the grown-up holds her wrist and watches the timer.
setup.caption: 4. Hold your breath with your face in the cold water.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of four rows and three counts in each row, and the middle count circled in each row.
setup.caption: 5. Circle the middle count in each row and compare.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Breath held, hand in cold water
Breath held, face in cold water

flow.do: Sit your child on a chair at a table. Find their pulse with two fingers on the inside of the wrist, below the thumb. Explain the three tests. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: You will hold your breath three ways: with nothing wet, with a hand in cold water and with your face in cold water. Will your heart beat faster, slower or the same each time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will hold your breath three ways. What will your heart do? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think your heart will do that?
good: Cold is a shock, so my heart will race.
Holding my breath is hard work.
My body might save air.
Seals slow down when they dive.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect the heart to race. If the wrist pulse is hard to find, press gently on the side of the neck, beside the windpipe. Practise one 15-second count before you go on.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cold Face Test. You guess what cold water will do to your heartbeat, before you test.

flow.do: Your child sits still and breathes normally for two minutes. Count the pulse for 15 seconds, three times, with a short pause between counts. Write down the three counts.
flow.say: Sit still and breathe as usual. I will count your pulse three times. This is your resting count.
flow.kid: Sit still. Breathe as usual. A grown-up counts your pulse three times.
flow.parent: A count of 18 to 26 in 15 seconds is usual for a child of nine who is sitting still.
flow.context: In this step of the Cold Face Test a grown-up counts your resting pulse three times.

flow.do: Test 1, breath held with nothing wet. Start the timer. Your child takes a normal breath in and holds it for 20 seconds. Count the pulse from second 5 to second 20. Rest one minute. Do this three times.
flow.say: Take a normal breath in and hold it. I will count from second 5 to second 20. Then you breathe and rest for one minute.
flow.kid: Breathe in and hold for 20 seconds. Then rest for one minute.
flow.parent: Say 'breathe' at 20 seconds. If 20 seconds is too long for your child, use 15 seconds for every test. Count from second 5 to second 15. Then compare only counts of the same length.
flow.context: In this step of the Cold Face Test you hold your breath with nothing wet, three times.

flow.do: Put the bowl on the table. Add the ice cubes or the fridge water and stir. Test the water with your own hand. It should feel as cold as water from the fridge. Your hand should be able to stay in for 20 seconds.
flow.say: I am making the water cold. Put one finger in. It should feel cold but it should not hurt.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the water cold. Dip one finger in to check.
flow.parent: If you have no fridge, use the coolest water you have, such as water from a clay pot. The change in the pulse will then be smaller.
flow.context: In this step of the Cold Face Test a grown-up cools the bowl of water with ice or fridge water.

flow.do: Test 2, hand in cold water. Your child takes a normal breath in, holds it and puts one hand in the water up to the wrist. Count the pulse on the other wrist from second 5 to second 20. Rest one minute. Do this three times.
flow.say: Breathe in, hold, and put this hand in the water. Keep it there until I say 'breathe'.
flow.kid: Hold your breath. Put one hand in the cold water for 20 seconds.
flow.parent: Dry the hand between tries. This test finds out whether cold on any part of the body changes the heartbeat.
flow.context: In this step of the Cold Face Test you hold your breath with one hand in cold water, three times.

flow.do: Test 3, face in cold water. Your child leans over the bowl, takes a normal breath in and lowers their face. The forehead, closed eyes, nose and cheeks go under. Hold their wrist and count from second 5 to second 20. Touch their shoulder twice at 20 seconds. Rest one minute. Do this three times.
flow.say: Breathe in, hold, and lower your face until your forehead and nose are under. Lift your face when I touch your shoulder twice. You can lift it sooner if you want to.
flow.kid: Hold your breath. Put your face in the water. Lift it when your shoulder is touched.
flow.parent: Keep the towel ready. If your child does not want to put their face in, soak a small towel in the cold water. Squeeze the towel lightly. They hold their breath, and you press the towel over their forehead, eyes and cheeks. The change is usually smaller this way. If the water has warmed up, add more ice first.

check.q: In the Cold Face Test, why do you also test a hand in cold water?
options: To see if cold on any body part works
To wash the hand
To make the water warmer
check.why: Suppose a cold hand does not slow the heart but a cold face does. Then the trigger is cold on the face. If you chose washing the hand, remember that each test changes one thing to find the trigger.

flow.context: In this step of the Cold Face Test you hold your breath with your face in cold water, three times.

flow.do: Put the three counts in each row in order of size and circle the middle one. Compare the four middle counts. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at the four middle counts. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which test changed your heartbeat most?
flow.kid: Circle the middle counts. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: What had to happen for your heart to slow down?
good: My face had to be in cold water.
Holding my breath alone did not do it.
The cold hand did not do it.

ask.q: Why might a slower heart help an animal who is under water?
good: The air in the body lasts longer.
A slow heart uses less oxygen.
A seal can stay down longer.

flow.parent: In most children the face-in-water count is 2 to 5 beats lower than the others. The breath-held count and the cold-hand count stay close to the resting count, or rise a little. Write down what you really found, even if it differs. If nothing changed, the water was probably not cold enough, or the count started too soon. The reason: cold water on the skin around the eyes and nose, together with a held breath, sets off the diving reflex. A nerve of the face carries the message, and the heart slows. Blood vessels in the arms and legs become narrower, so more blood stays with the brain and the heart. The oxygen from one breath then lasts longer. Seals, dolphins, ducks and humans all have this reflex. Your child did not learn it and did not plan it.
flow.think: You may never dive for your food. So why does your body have a reflex for diving?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cold Face Test. You compare your pulse counts and say what set off the change.

experiments.title: The Big Eyes Test: which drawn face do people find cuter?
experiments.question: Two drawn faces differ in one thing only. Do most people call the face with bigger eyes cuter? Do most people call the face with the eyes lower down cuter?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In each pair, which face will get more votes for being cuter? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The two faces in a pair differ in one thing only, so draw everything else the same. Ask every voter the same question in the same words. Swap which card is on the left for each new voter, because some people tend to pick one side. Ask each voter alone, so that nobody copies. Ask at least 8 voters, because two or three people can agree by chance.

materials.item: cards of the same size, made by cutting a notebook page into four
a steel tumbler about 7 centimetres across, to trace the heads
a 1-rupee coin, to trace the big eyes
a pencil and a ruler
voters: family, neighbours, friends, or relatives on a video call

experiments.record: Draw a table with two rows, one for each pair. For each voter, put one stroke under the card they chose.
experiments.context: In this experiment you draw two pairs of faces. The faces in a pair differ in one thing only. You ask at least 8 people which face is cuter, and count the votes.

setup.art: Four paper cards on a table, each with a pencil circle traced round a steel tumbler.
setup.caption: 1. Trace the same head circle on four cards.

setup.art: Two cards side by side: face A with two small dot eyes on the middle line, face B with two large round eyes on the middle line, and the same small nose and mouth on both.
setup.caption: 2. Pair 1: small eyes on card A, big eyes on card B.

setup.art: Two cards side by side: face C with eyes high up near the top of the circle, face D with the same eyes low down and the nose and mouth close below them.
setup.caption: 3. Pair 2: eyes high on card C, eyes low on card D.

setup.art: A child holding up two cards in front of an older woman, who is pointing at one of them.
setup.caption: 4. Ask each voter: which face is cuter?

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of two rows and tally strokes under each card letter.
setup.caption: 5. Count the votes for each card.

flow.do: Trace the tumbler on all four cards. Draw a faint line across the middle of circles A and B. On A, draw two filled dots on the line, each as wide as the flat end of the pencil. On B, trace the coin twice on the line and fill in a dark centre. Add the same dot nose and the same short curved mouth to both. Ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: These two faces differ in one thing only, the size of the eyes. We will ask 8 people which is cuter. Which face do you think will get more votes? Why?
flow.kid: Draw face A with small eyes. Draw face B with big eyes. Which will win? Why?
flow.parent: Check that the nose and mouth are in the same place on both cards. Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Big Eyes Test. You draw the first pair of faces and guess which one people will call cuter.

flow.do: On C and D, draw eyes 1 centimetre wide. On C, put the eyes 2 centimetres below the top of the circle. Put the nose 2 centimetres lower, and the mouth near the bottom. On D, put the eyes 4 and a half centimetres below the top. Put the nose and mouth close under the eyes.
flow.say: These two faces have the same eyes. On C the eyes sit high. On D they sit low, and there is a big forehead above them. Which will get more votes, and why?
flow.kid: Draw face C with high eyes. Draw face D with low eyes. Guess again.
flow.context: In this step of the Big Eyes Test you draw the second pair of faces. They differ only in how high the eyes sit.

flow.do: Ask at least 8 voters, one at a time. Hold up cards A and B and ask the question. Record the vote. Then hold up C and D and ask again. Swap the left and right cards for each new voter.
flow.say: Here are two faces. Which face is cuter? Please point to one.
flow.kid: Ask each voter: which face is cuter? Put a stroke for each vote.
flow.parent: Voters must not hear each other's answers. A photo of each pair sent by phone also works. If a voter asks what 'cuter' means, say 'whichever you feel like calling cute'. You can spread this step over the day.
flow.context: In this step of the Big Eyes Test you ask at least 8 people to vote on each pair.

flow.do: Count the votes for each card. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below. Then find one soft toy or cartoon character at home and look at its eyes and forehead.
flow.say: Count the votes. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Now look at this toy. What has the toy maker done to the eyes and the head?
flow.kid: Count the votes. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Real babies have big eyes that sit low on the face. Why might adults find that cute?
good: It makes adults want to look after babies.
Babies need a lot of care.
It could be a trigger, like the red spot for a gull chick.

ask.q: With 8 voters, how many votes for one card would be strong evidence?
good: Seven or eight.
Much more than four, because four is what chance gives.

flow.parent: In most groups, B and D win clearly. If your votes are close to four against four, ask more people. The reason: babies have big eyes, set low on a large head with a high forehead. In 1943 Konrad Lorenz proposed that these features work as a sign stimulus, and set off caring in adults. Toys and cartoons make the eyes bigger still, which makes them a supernormal stimulus. Scientists still argue about how much of this response is inborn and how much is learned from toys and cartoons.

check.q: In the Big Eyes Test, why do the two faces in a pair differ in one thing only?
options: So we know which feature changed the votes
So the drawing is quicker
So the voters get confused
check.why: If the faces differed in eye size and mouth shape, you could not tell which one mattered. Changing one thing at a time is what makes the test fair. If you chose a quicker drawing, remember that the point is to find the trigger.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Big Eyes Test. You count the votes and say which features people called cuter.

activities.title: Find the Trigger: three reflexes in twelve minutes

materials.item: a clear plastic folder or a clear box lid. A closed glass window also works
a pair of socks rolled into a soft ball
a pencil with a blunt end
a wedge of lemon, or a small piece of tamarind
a notebook page

schedule.what: Set off three reflexes and write down the stimulus and the response of each.

activities.record: A table with three rows: blink, toe curl and mouth-watering. For each one, write the stimulus, the response and whether you could stop it.
activities.context: In this activity you set off three reflexes in your own body: a blink, a toe curl and mouth-watering. For each one you find the stimulus that sets it off.

setup.art: A child holding a clear plastic folder in front of her face while a grown-up two steps away throws a rolled sock ball gently at the folder.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a clear sheet in front of your face. A helper throws a sock ball at it.

setup.art: A child sitting with one bare foot on a grown-up's knee, and the grown-up stroking the sole from heel to toes with the blunt end of a pencil.
setup.caption: 2. A helper strokes the sole of your foot with a blunt pencil.

setup.art: A child with her tongue out and a grown-up squeezing one drop from a lemon wedge onto the tip of her tongue.
setup.caption: 3. Put one drop of lemon juice on your tongue.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of three rows headed Reflex, Stimulus and Response.
setup.caption: 4. Write down the stimulus and the response for each.

flow.do: Your child holds the clear sheet about 10 centimetres in front of their face. Stand two steps away. Ask for a guess. Then throw the sock ball gently at the sheet five times. Count the blinks.
flow.say: This sheet will stop the sock ball every time, and you know that. Do you think you will blink? Why? Try your best not to.
flow.kid: Hold the clear sheet. The sock ball cannot reach you. Will you blink?

ask.q: You knew the sock ball could not hit you. So what made you blink?
good: Something was flying at my eyes.
My eyes shut before I could think.
The blink did not wait for me.

flow.parent: Most children blink at four or five throws out of five. If you have no clear sheet, your child can stand close behind a closed glass window. You throw from the other side.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Trigger. You find out whether you blink at a sock ball that cannot hit you.

flow.do: Stroke the sole of one bare foot firmly from heel to toes with the blunt end of the pencil. Watch the toes. Then your child swallows once, and you put one drop of lemon juice on the tip of the tongue.
flow.say: Watch your toes while I stroke your sole. What did they do? Now swallow, and put your tongue out. What happens in your mouth after the lemon drop?
flow.kid: Watch your toes. Then taste one lemon drop. What does your mouth do?
flow.parent: The toes usually curl down. A ticklish child may pull the whole foot away, which is another reflex. After the lemon drop the mouth fills with saliva within a few seconds.
flow.context: In this step of Find the Trigger you set off a toe curl and mouth-watering.

flow.do: Fill in the table together. For each reflex, write the stimulus and the response. Ask whether your child planned any of the three.
flow.say: Each reflex had a stimulus of its own. Would the lemon drop make you blink? Would the sock ball make your mouth water? Did you plan any of these?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Which stimulus set off which response?

check.q: In Find the Trigger, what was the stimulus for the blink?
options: The sock ball rushing at the eyes
The eyelids shutting
The clear sheet
check.why: The stimulus is what sets the reflex off, and here that was something rushing at the eyes. The eyelids shutting is the response. If you chose the sheet, remember that the sheet was there the whole time and caused no blink by itself.

flow.context: This is the last step of Find the Trigger. You match each of the three reflexes to its stimulus.

activities.title: The Swallow Test: a pattern that runs to the end

materials.item: a tumbler of drinking water
a phone timer or a clock that shows seconds

schedule.what: Try to stop a swallow halfway, then count swallows with and without water.

activities.record: Write whether you could stop a swallow halfway. Then write two numbers: swallows in 30 seconds with no water, and swallows in 30 seconds with small sips.
activities.context: In this activity you test your own swallow. A swallow is a fixed action pattern: it needs a trigger, and once it starts it runs to the end.

setup.art: A child with a tumbler of water in one hand and the fingers of her other hand resting lightly on the front of her throat.
setup.caption: 1. Rest your fingers on your throat. Take a sip and swallow.

setup.art: The same child with an empty mouth and a look of effort, with a timer beside her showing 30 seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Swallow as many times as you can in 30 seconds, with no water.

setup.art: The child taking a small sip from the tumbler, with the timer beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Do it again with a small sip for each swallow. Compare the two counts.

flow.do: Your child rests two fingers on the front of the throat and takes a small sip of water. Ask for a guess. Then they start to swallow and try to stop halfway. Try three times.
flow.say: Feel the bump in your throat go up and down when you swallow. Do you think you can stop a swallow halfway? Why? Try it.
flow.kid: Feel your throat. Start a swallow. Can you stop halfway?
flow.parent: Nobody can stop it. Once water reaches the back of the mouth, the rest of the swallow runs by itself.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Swallow Test. You find out whether a swallow can be stopped halfway.

flow.do: Your child empties their mouth. Ask for a guess. Time 30 seconds while they swallow as many times as they can with no water. Count the throat bumps. Rest one minute. Then time 30 seconds with a small sip for every swallow.
flow.say: How many times can you swallow in 30 seconds with nothing in your mouth? Guess first. Then we try with a sip each time.
flow.kid: Swallow with no water for 30 seconds. Then swallow with sips. Count both.
flow.parent: Most people manage only 4 to 8 dry swallows and find that each one gets harder. With sips, 10 or more is easy. Small sips only, so that nobody chokes.
flow.context: In this step of the Swallow Test you count your swallows with no water and then with sips of water.

flow.do: Compare the two counts. Talk about the questions below. After your child has answered, read them the note.
flow.say: Why was it so hard to swallow with nothing in your mouth? What does a swallow need before it will start?
flow.kid: Which count was bigger? What does a swallow need to start?

ask.q: What is the trigger for a swallow?
good: Something touching the back of the mouth.
Water or food or saliva to swallow.
Without anything there, it will not start.

flow.parent: The trigger for a swallow is food, water or saliva touching the back of the mouth. With no water, the saliva soon runs out and the trigger is missing. Once a swallow starts, more than 20 muscles work in a set order, and the order cannot be stopped halfway. A goose rolling an egg shows the same two features: a trigger, and a pattern that runs to the end.

check.q: Which two things are true of a fixed action pattern, such as a swallow?
options: It needs a trigger and runs to the end
It needs practice and a teacher
It is slow and can stop anywhere
check.why: In the Swallow Test, a swallow would not start without something to swallow, and it could not be stopped halfway. Those are the two marks of a fixed action pattern. Nobody practises swallowing with a teacher.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Swallow Test. You compare the two counts and say what a swallow needs to start.

activities.title: When Does the Window Close? Draw the ducklings' graph

materials.item: a page of squared paper from a maths notebook
a pencil and a ruler

schedule.what: Draw a line graph of imprinting at eight ages and mark the sensitive period.

activities.record: A line graph with age in hours along the bottom and ducklings who imprinted, out of 10, up the side. Shade the part of the graph where 6 or more ducklings imprinted.
activities.context: In this activity you draw a graph of how many ducklings imprint at each age. The numbers are made up, but they follow the pattern that Eckhard Hess found with mallard ducklings in 1959.

setup.art: A model duck on a short arm moving round a circular track, with one small duckling walking after the model.
setup.caption: 1. Each duckling met a moving model duck once, at one age.

setup.art: A page of squared paper with two axes drawn: eight age groups along the bottom and the numbers 0 to 10 up the side.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the two lines of the graph and label them.

setup.art: The same graph with eight dots joined by a line that rises to a peak and falls to zero, and the peak shaded.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the eight points, join them and shade the peak.

flow.do: Read the table of numbers together. Explain that each group of 10 ducklings met the moving model once, at one age. The next day each duckling could follow the model or not. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Each group of ducklings met the model duck at a different age. At which age do you think most ducklings imprinted? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the table. At which age did most ducklings imprint? Guess first.

chart.title: Made-up numbers that follow the pattern Hess found
cols: Age when the duckling first met the model, in hours

ask.q: Why might the very youngest ducklings imprint less than those of 14 hours?
good: They can hardly walk yet.
They are still drying and resting.
They cannot follow well in the first hours.

flow.context: This is the first step of When Does the Window Close. You read the table of ducklings and guess the best age for imprinting.

flow.do: Your child draws a line along the bottom of the page and marks the eight age groups, 2 squares apart. They draw a line up the side and mark 0 to 10, one square each. They put a dot for each group and join the dots with a ruler.
flow.say: Put the ages along the bottom and the number of ducklings up the side. One dot for each age group. Then join the dots.
flow.kid: Draw the two lines. Put one dot for each age. Join the dots.

chart.title: Made-up numbers that follow the pattern Hess found
cols: Age when the duckling first met the model, in hours

flow.parent: The numbers in order are 3, 4, 6, 9, 6, 4, 2 and 0. The line should climb to a peak at 13 to 16 hours and then fall to zero.
flow.context: In this step of When Does the Window Close you draw the line graph from the table.

flow.do: Your child shades the part of the graph where 6 or more ducklings imprinted. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Shade where 6 or more imprinted. That is the middle of the sensitive period. What does the graph say about a duckling who hatches alone and meets nobody for two days?
flow.kid: Shade the peak. What happens to a duckling who meets nobody for two days?

ask.q: In nature, why is one day long enough?
good: The mother is right there when they hatch.
They leave the nest with her on the first or second day.

flow.parent: The peak covers about 9 to 20 hours. In Hess's real tests, ducklings older than about 30 hours hardly imprinted at all. Many of them had begun to fear new things by then, and moved away from the model.

check.q: On the ducklings' graph, the line is highest at 13 to 16 hours and at zero by 32 hours. What does this show?
options: Imprinting works only for a short time
Older ducklings imprint best
Age makes no difference
check.why: The line rises, peaks in the first day and falls to zero. So there is a short sensitive period for imprinting. If you chose 'older ducklings imprint best', look again at the right-hand end of the graph.

flow.context: This is the last step of When Does the Window Close. You mark the sensitive period on your graph and say what it means.

projects.title: The Yawn Spread: does seeing a yawn set off a yawn?

materials.item: a notebook page for the log
a clock or phone timer
volunteers aged six or older: family, neighbours or friends

schedule.what: Watch for yawns at home and log what came just before each one.
Yawn in front of six people, one at a time, and count who yawns.
Smile in front of the same six people, count yawns, and compare.

projects.record: Day 1: a log of yawns, with the time and what came before. Days 2 and 3: a table with six rows, one for each volunteer, and a tick if they yawned within three minutes.
projects.context: In this three-day project you find out whether seeing a yawn sets off a yawn in other people. A yawn is a fixed action pattern in humans.

setup.art: A family in a living room in the evening, one person yawning widely and a child on the sofa writing in a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: log every yawn you see, and what came just before it.

setup.art: A child sitting opposite an older man and giving a huge yawn with her hand half over her mouth.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: yawn three times in front of each volunteer. Watch for three minutes.

setup.art: The same child smiling widely at the same man, with a notebook table beside her showing ticks and crosses.
setup.caption: 3. Day 3: smile three times instead. Compare the two counts.

flow.do: Day 1. In the evening, your child watches the family for an hour while doing other things. For every yawn they see, they log the time and what came just before. They also try to stop one of their own yawns halfway.
flow.say: Today we collect yawns. Each time someone yawns, write the time and what happened just before. Did that person see or hear another yawn?
flow.kid: Log every yawn you see. Write what came just before it.
flow.parent: Late evening gives the most yawns. A yawn lasts about six seconds, and most people find that they cannot stop one halfway.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Yawn Spread. You watch for yawns at home and log what came before each one.

flow.do: Day 2. Your child tests six volunteers, one at a time, without saying what the test is about. They sit facing the volunteer and chat. Over one minute they give three big, slow yawns. Then they watch for three minutes and record a tick for a yawn.
flow.say: Do not tell them what we are testing. Yawn three times, slowly, where they can see you. Then keep chatting and watch for three minutes.
flow.kid: Yawn three times in front of each person. Watch for three minutes.
flow.wait: Do this the day after the yawn log
flow.parent: Choose volunteers aged six or older. Children younger than about five rarely catch a yawn. A stifled yawn with the mouth shut counts as a yawn.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Yawn Spread. You yawn in front of six people and count who yawns back.

flow.do: Day 3. Your child tests the same six people at about the same time of day. This time they give three big smiles in one minute and watch for three minutes. Then they compare the two counts and tell the volunteers what the test was.
flow.say: Today you smile three times, and we count yawns again. If people yawn as often after smiles, the yawns were not caught from you.
flow.kid: Smile three times in front of each person. Count yawns. Compare the days.
flow.wait: Do this on the third day, at about the same time of day

ask.q: Why did you need the day of smiles?
good: People yawn anyway when they are tired.
To check that it was the yawn that did it.
It is the comparison that makes the test fair.

flow.parent: In Robert Provine's tests, about half of adults yawned while watching yawns, and far fewer while watching smiles. With six volunteers your numbers may differ. Two or three yawns after yawning and none or one after smiling is a usual result. Nobody yet knows why yawns spread.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Yawn Spread. You smile in front of the same six people and compare the yawn counts.

challenges.title: The Crane Puppet: feed a chick who must never see a human
challenges.problem: Keepers who raise crane chicks for release into the wild have a problem. A chick who sees humans in her first days may imprint on humans, and never join other cranes. So the keepers wear a plain costume and feed the chick with a hand puppet shaped like a crane's head. Your problem is the same. Build a crane-head puppet. Use the puppet to move 10 groundnuts from the table into a cup. A helper plays the chick and watches for any sign of a human.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
The puppet must cover your hand and your arm up to the elbow.
The chick must not see your skin or your face, or hear your voice.
Move 10 groundnuts into the cup in two minutes.
Each time the chick spots a human, you lose one groundnut from the cup.
materials: a long sock, grey or white if you have one
stiff paper or thin cardboard for the beak
two clothes pegs or a pair of kitchen tongs
a red sketch pen or a scrap of red cloth
a bedsheet or a dupatta to hide behind
10 groundnuts in their shells, or 10 rajma beans, and a cup
general: Pull the sock over your hand. Your thumb is the lower beak and your fingers are the upper beak.
Tape two long cardboard triangles to the sock as a beak.
Hold a clothes peg inside the tip of the sock, so that the beak can grip.
creative: Hold kitchen tongs inside the sock, to make a long beak like a real crane's.
Hang a bedsheet over a table and push the puppet through a gap, so that only the crane shows.
Play a recording of crane calls from a phone hidden under the sheet. Real keepers play crane calls to their chicks.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own puppet. A sarus crane has a grey body and a bare red head and upper neck. Decide which features a crane chick most needs to see. Draw your design, build it and test it with 10 groundnuts in two minutes. Write how many reached the cup and how many times the chick spotted a human.
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a crane-head hand puppet and feed a pretend chick. The chick must not see or hear a human. Real keepers do this so that crane chicks do not imprint on people.

setup.art: A keeper covered from head to foot in a loose white costume, holding out a hand puppet shaped like a crane's head towards a small brown crane chick.
setup.caption: 1. Real keepers hide in a costume and feed crane chicks with a puppet.

setup.art: A child's arm inside a grey sock with a cardboard beak and a red patch on top, picking up a groundnut from a table.
setup.caption: 2. Build a crane-head puppet that covers your arm to the elbow.

setup.art: A bedsheet hung over a table with the sock puppet poking through a gap and dropping a groundnut into a cup, while a grown-up sits opposite and watches.
setup.caption: 3. Move 10 groundnuts into the cup. The chick must not spot a human.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask what the chick must never see or hear. Ask which features of a crane the puppet needs most.
flow.say: A crane chick imprints in her first days. What must she never see or hear? What should she see when she is fed?
flow.kid: The chick must imprint on a crane. What must she never see?

ask.q: Which features of a parent crane might matter most to a chick?
good: A long beak.
The red head.
Movement near the food.
The call.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Crane Puppet. You work out what a crane chick must and must not see.

flow.do: Your child chooses a design and builds the puppet. Check that it covers the arm up to the elbow and that the beak can pick up one groundnut.
flow.say: Build your puppet. The beak has to grip one groundnut at a time. Test the grip before we start the clock.
flow.kid: Build your puppet. Check that the beak can grip a groundnut.
flow.parent: Let your child try their own idea first, even if it looks likely to fail. A clothes peg or tongs inside the sock helps a small hand to grip.
flow.context: In this step of the Crane Puppet you build the puppet and test the beak's grip.

flow.do: Test it. You are the chick. Sit at the table and watch closely. Time two minutes while your child moves the groundnuts with the puppet. Say 'human' each time you see skin or a face, or hear a voice.
flow.say: I am the chick. You have two minutes and ten groundnuts. If I see or hear a human, I will say 'human'.
flow.kid: Move ten groundnuts with the puppet. Stay hidden and silent.
flow.context: In this step of the Crane Puppet you test the puppet for two minutes while a helper plays the chick.

flow.do: Count the groundnuts in the cup and take one out for each 'human'. Your child changes one thing and tests again. Then talk about the question below.
flow.say: What gave you away? Change one thing and try again. Why do keepers go to so much trouble for one chick?
flow.kid: What gave you away? Change one thing. Test again.

ask.q: What might happen to a crane who imprinted on humans?
good: She would walk up to people and could get hurt.
She might not join other cranes.
She might not choose a crane as a mate.

flow.parent: Praise a clear account of what went wrong as much as a full cup. Keepers of whooping cranes in North America have used costumes and puppets like this for many years.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Crane Puppet. You improve the puppet and say why keepers hide from crane chicks.

items.p: What is a reflex?
opts: A fast, automatic response to a stimulus
A plan made by the brain
items.why: A reflex is fast and automatic, and nobody has to learn it. A skill learned by practice, such as cycling, is the opposite kind of thing.

items.p: A drop of lemon juice makes your mouth water. Which one is the stimulus?
items.why: The stimulus is what sets the reflex off. The saliva flowing is the response. The tongue is where the sensors are.

items.p: A goose's egg is taken away halfway through a roll. What does she do?
items.why: A fixed action pattern usually runs to the end once it has started. Lorenz and Tinbergen saw the goose draw her beak back to the nest with no egg.

items.p: What does a newly hatched gosling imprint on?
opts: The first big moving thing she sees
The biggest egg in the nest
items.why: A gosling fixes on the first large moving thing near her in her first day. In nature that is her mother.

items.p: What is a sign stimulus?
opts: The one feature that sets off a behaviour
A reward given after a trick
items.why: A sign stimulus is one feature, such as the red spot on a gull's beak. The animal responds to that feature more than to the whole thing.

items.p: The short time early in life when imprinting can happen is called the ____ period.
items.why: It is called the sensitive period. Some books call it the critical period. For a mallard duckling this period is about the first day after hatching.

items.p: A behaviour that an animal can do from birth, without being taught, is called ____.
items.why: Innate and inborn mean the same thing: present from birth or hatching, with no teaching.

items.p: A fixed action pattern has to be practised many times before it works.
items.why: False. A fixed action pattern works the first time. A squirrel raised with no soil and no nuts still made burying movements.

items.p: Humans have a reflex that is also found in seals and ducks.
items.why: True. The diving reflex slows the heart of a human, a seal and a duck. The trigger is cold water on the face.

items.p: Match each reflex to its stimulus.
pairs: Cold water on the face, with the breath held
items.why: Each reflex has a stimulus of its own. A stimulus for one reflex does not set off another.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one a reflex, or a fixed action pattern?
items: the hand pulling back from heat
items.why: A reflex is one quick response of one body part. A fixed action pattern is a longer set of movements in a set order.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how the blink reflex works.
items: Sensors in the eye pick it up
A message runs along a nerve to the lowest part of the brain
A message runs back to the eyelid muscles
a: Sensors in the eye pick it up
A message runs along a nerve to the lowest part of the brain
A message runs back to the eyelid muscles
items.why: A reflex starts with a stimulus and a sensor. The message goes in along one nerve and out along another. A muscle pulls last.

items.p: In the Cold Face Test, a cold face slowed the heart. A cold hand did not. What does that show?
items.a: It shows that the trigger for the diving reflex is cold water on the face. Cold on other parts of the body does not set it off.
items.why: A strong answer says that only one thing differed between the two tests, the body part in the water. So that body part is what mattered.

items.p: A gosling's rule is 'follow the first big moving thing'. Explain in two sentences why this rule works in nature.
items.a: In nature the first big moving thing a gosling sees is her mother. The mother is sitting on the nest when the eggs hatch. So the simple rule nearly always leads her to the right bird.
items.why: A strong answer says who is beside the nest at hatching. It also says that the rule only fails when a person interferes.

items.p: Draw the two faces of one pair from the Big Eyes Test. Circle the one thing that differs.
items.a: Two round faces that are the same except for one feature: either small eyes and big eyes, or eyes high and eyes low. The differing feature is circled.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the head, nose and mouth the same on both faces. Only then can the votes be put down to the one feature that changed.
items.art: Two empty circles side by side for the child to draw faces in.

items.p: A hen ignores a chick she can see but cannot hear. What is the trigger for her rescue?
items.why: She runs to a cheeping chick even when she cannot see them. So the sound is the trigger, more than the sight.

items.p: Why can a dummy set off an inborn behaviour?
opts: It has the one feature that matters
It is bigger than the animal
items.why: The animal responds to the sign stimulus. Any dummy that carries that feature, such as a red spot, can set off the behaviour.

items.p: A duckling first sees a moving thing at 40 hours old. What will most likely happen?
opts: She will not imprint on it
She will imprint twice as strongly
She will forget how to walk
items.why: The sensitive period for a mallard duckling is nearly over by 30 hours. At 40 hours she is more likely to move away from a new thing.

items.p: Why is a reflex faster than an action you plan?
opts: The message skips the brain's planning parts
Reflex nerves are outside the body
items.why: In a reflex the message goes in to the spinal cord or lower brain. Then it goes straight back out to a muscle. A planned action takes a longer path.

items.p: A cold hand sets off the diving reflex as well as a cold face does.
items.why: False. The sensors that set off the diving reflex are in the skin of the face, around the eyes and nose.

items.p: A koel raised by crows grows up cawing like a crow.
items.why: False. Every koel is raised by crows or other foster birds, and every koel still calls like a koel. The call is innate.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one innate, or learned?
items: a cuckoo chick pushing eggs out
a newborn baby turning to a touch on the cheek
what a gosling's parent looks like
items.why: The urge to follow is innate, but whom to follow is learned by imprinting. Imprinting is learning, though it happens only once and very early.

items.p: Three of these are supernormal stimuli. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: A red stick with white bands
A cartoon face with huge eyes
items.why: The giant egg, the striped stick and the cartoon face are made-up triggers that are stronger than the real thing. A real beak is the normal stimulus.

items.p: A seal's heart beats 10 times a minute on a dive. How many beats is that in a 12-minute dive?
items.why: 10 beats each minute for 12 minutes is 10 times 12, which is 120 beats. At 100 beats a minute it would have been 1,200.

items.p: Put the steps of Konrad Lorenz's goose test in order.
items: Split one clutch of goose eggs into two groups
The goose hatches one group, and Lorenz hatches the other
Each gosling sees a different first moving thing
Each gosling goes to the one she saw first
a: Split one clutch of goose eggs into two groups
The goose hatches one group, and Lorenz hatches the other
Each gosling sees a different first moving thing
Each gosling goes to the one she saw first
items.why: The eggs came from one clutch, so the goslings were alike. Only the first thing they saw differed. That makes it a fair test of imprinting.

items.p: A toy maker wants a soft toy that people want to hug. Which features should she change, and why?
items.a: She should give the toy a big head, a high forehead, big eyes set low and round cheeks. These are baby features, and people find them cute and want to care for them.
items.why: A strong answer names at least two baby features. It links them to the caring response, or to the votes in the Big Eyes Test.

items.p: An oystercatcher chooses a giant egg that she cannot cover. Explain why her rule works in nature but fails here.
items.a: Her rule is to sit on the biggest egg. In nature no egg is too big, so the rule never goes wrong. A giant egg made by a scientist is bigger than any real egg. Her rule has no upper limit, so she keeps choosing the bigger egg.
items.why: A strong answer states the bird's rule, and says that nature never offers an egg that big.

items.p: A swallow cannot be stopped halfway. Why might that be useful?
items.a: Food or water that stopped halfway could slip into the windpipe and choke the animal. A swallow that always finishes moves it safely past.
items.why: A strong answer names a danger of stopping in the middle. Any sensible danger is accepted.

items.p: A wetland centre plans to raise crane chicks by hand and release them. People disagree about how.

views.says: We must wear costumes and feed the chicks with crane puppets. It is slow and costly. But chicks who imprint on people cannot live as wild cranes.
Let visitors hold and feed the chicks. People who have held a crane chick will give money to protect cranes.
Cranes who follow people will walk into our fields and villages. They will be hurt, or they will eat our crop.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about imprinting. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that imprinting happens in the first days and is very hard to undo. So a chick handled by visitors may never join wild cranes. A fair answer to the tourism officer is that visitors could watch through a window.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses the fact that imprinting is early and lasting. It also takes the need for money and the farmer's worry seriously.

items.p: Label the four parts of a reflex on this drawing of a hand touching a hot tumbler.
labels: Nerve carrying the message out to the muscle
a: Sensor in the skin: at the fingertip touching the tumbler
Nerve carrying the message in: from the fingertip up the arm
Nerve carrying the message out to the muscle: from the spinal cord down to the arm muscle
items.why: The message goes in along one nerve and out along another. It turns round in the spinal cord, without waiting for the planning parts of the brain.
items.art: A side view of a child from the waist up, with one fingertip on a steaming tumbler, the arm, the backbone and the upper arm muscle outlined, and four blank label lines.

items.p: A stickleback attacks a red wax lump and leaves a lifelike grey model alone. What does this show?
opts: A red underside is the trigger
items.why: The lump had only one fish-like feature, the red underside, and the lump was attacked. The lifelike model lacked red and was left alone.

items.p: Duck embryos who hear no calls in the egg later fail to pick their mother's call. What does this suggest?
opts: Hearing calls inside the egg matters
Calls are learned after a year
items.why: Gilbert Gottlieb's tests showed that even an instinct can need an experience. Here the experience is the duckling's own voice, heard inside the egg.

items.p: In the Cold Face Test, why is the pulse counted three times for each test?
opts: One count can be wrong by chance
The heart needs to warm up
The water gets colder each time
items.why: A single count can be off by a beat or two. Three counts show whether the result repeats, and the middle count is a fair one to use.

items.p: Mice raised in cages still dig the burrow shape of their own kind. What does this show?
items.why: The mice had never seen a burrow or another mouse digging. So the shape did not come from copying or teaching.

items.p: A supernormal stimulus works because the animal's rule has no upper limit.
items.why: True. A rule such as 'sit on the biggest egg' never needed a limit. Nature never offers an egg that is too big.

items.p: Imprinting is the same as learning by practice, only faster.
items.why: False. Imprinting needs no practice and no reward. It happens only in a short sensitive period, and it is very hard to undo.

items.p: Match each test to what it shows.
pairs: Take the egg away halfway through a roll
A fixed pattern runs to the end
Offer a bird a giant egg
A stronger trigger can beat the real one
Hatch goslings away from their mother
What a parent looks like is learned
Raise a squirrel with no soil or nuts
items.why: Each test removes or changes one thing and watches what the animal still does. That is how inborn and learned parts are told apart.

items.p: A resting pulse is 88 beats a minute. It slows by one quarter. What is the new pulse?
items.why: One quarter of 88 is 22. 88 minus 22 is 66 beats a minute.

items.p: A made-up trigger that works better than the real thing is called a ____ stimulus.
items.why: Supernormal means 'beyond normal'. A giant egg and a cartoon face with huge eyes are supernormal stimuli.

items.p: Does a duckling follow colour or movement? Describe the dummies you would use to find out.
items.a: I would show one group a red ball that moves and another group the same red ball kept still. Then I would show a grey ball that moves. If ducklings follow both moving balls and not the still one, movement matters and colour does not.
items.why: A strong answer changes one feature at a time and keeps the rest the same. It also says what result would point to each answer.

items.p: Give one reason why finding baby faces cute might be inborn. Give one reason why this might be learned.
items.a: Inborn: children as young as three, and people in many countries, respond to baby features. Learned: children grow up with big-eyed toys and cartoons, so they may learn what counts as cute.
items.why: A strong answer gives evidence on both sides, and does not claim that the question is settled.

items.p: A reflex cannot be switched off by deciding. Name one way this helps you and one way this causes trouble.
items.a: It helps because my hand leaves a hot tumbler before I have time to think. It could be a problem when a doctor needs me to keep my eye open and I blink anyway.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real case of each. Any sensible examples are accepted.

items.p: You have the diving reflex, though you may never dive for food. Explain how you came to have it.
items.a: I inherited it from my parents through DNA, as they did from theirs. Seals, ducks and humans all have it, so scientists think it comes from ancestors that all of us share.
items.why: A strong answer says the reflex is inherited and not learned. It uses the fact that many kinds of animals share this reflex.

items.p: On her first day, a duckling turns towards the call of her own kind of mother. Scientists explain this differently.

views.says: It is an instinct, inherited whole. Nobody taught her, and she had never heard a mother duck.
It grew. She heard her own voice inside the egg, and without that she would not pick the right call.
Both are right. She inherits a body that learns this from her own voice, almost every time.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say what test could help to decide.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that Gottlieb's ducklings failed to pick the call when they heard nothing in the egg. A useful test is to change what the embryo hears and see which call the duckling later prefers.
items.why: Working scientists hold each of these views. A strong answer uses the egg test, and suggests changing one thing before hatching.

items.p: Draw a dummy that a gull chick would peck at more than a real beak. Label what you made stronger.
items.a: A long thin shape that is redder than a real beak, with strong bands or a large red patch. Labels point to the stronger redness, the thinness or the contrast.
items.why: A chick responds to a shape that is red, long, thin and high in contrast. A strong drawing makes at least one of these stronger than in a real beak.
items.art: A blank box with a small outline of a gull chick looking up at an empty space.

quiz.p: Which of these is a reflex?
opts: Blinking when something flies at your eye
quiz.why: A blink at something rushing towards the eye is fast, automatic and unlearned. The other three are learned or chosen.

quiz.p: What sets off a reflex or a fixed action pattern?
quiz.why: Each reflex and each fixed pattern waits for a stimulus of its own, also called a trigger.

quiz.p: Which sentence is true of a fixed action pattern?
opts: Once started, it usually runs to the end
quiz.why: A goose finishes the rolling movement even when the egg has gone. Humans have fixed patterns too, such as swallowing.

quiz.p: A cuckoo chick pushes eggs out of the nest a day after hatching. What kind of behaviour is this?
opts: A trick taught by the foster mother
quiz.why: The chick is blind and has never seen this done, so the behaviour cannot be copied or taught. It is an instinct.

quiz.p: A gull chick pecks more at a model beak that has a red spot. What is the red spot?
quiz.why: The red spot is the one feature that sets off pecking. That makes it the sign stimulus.

quiz.p: With the breath held and the face in cold water, a person's heart usually:
quiz.why: This is the diving reflex. In humans the heart usually slows by a tenth to a quarter.

quiz.p: How does the diving reflex help a seal?
opts: Her oxygen lasts longer under water
quiz.why: A slow heart and narrow blood vessels in the limbs save oxygen for the brain and heart. So one breath lasts longer.

quiz.p: Goslings hatched by Konrad Lorenz followed him and not adult geese. Why?
opts: He was the first moving thing they saw
He gave them the best food
quiz.why: The goslings imprinted on the first large moving thing near them, and that was Lorenz. No rewards or training were needed.

quiz.p: When can a mallard duckling imprint?
opts: Only in a short time after hatching
quiz.why: Imprinting has a sensitive period. For mallard ducklings this period peaks at 13 to 16 hours and is nearly over by 30 hours.

quiz.p: An oystercatcher chooses a giant egg over her own. What is the giant egg?
quiz.why: The giant egg is a made-up trigger that works better than the real one. That is a supernormal stimulus.

quiz.p: An animal who has strong instincts can also learn.
quiz.why: True. A bird builds her first nest with inborn movements and builds better nests with practice. Instinct gives a start, and learning adds to it.

quiz.p: A duckling hatches with the urge to follow. What must she still learn?
quiz.why: The urge and the movements are innate. Which bird to follow is learned by imprinting in the first day.

open_questions.q: How does DNA build the wiring for a whole behaviour, such as digging a burrow with an escape tunnel?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have linked a few regions of DNA to parts of some behaviours. Nobody can yet follow every step from a gene to a movement.

open_questions.q: What is a duckling's experience while she imprints?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can see which part of the brain changes, and what the duckling does afterwards. Nobody has a way to find out what it is like for her.

open_questions.q: Why do yawns spread from one person to another?
open_questions.why_open: About half of adults yawn after seeing yawns. Some scientists link this to feeling close to others, and some link it to staying alert together. The evidence does not settle it.

open_questions.q: Is the human response to baby faces present from birth?
open_questions.why_open: Children of three already respond to baby features. Testing younger babies is hard, and children see big-eyed toys from their first months.

open_questions.q: What closes a sensitive period, and can one be opened again?
open_questions.why_open: Some changes in the brain that end a sensitive period are known. Whether a closed period can safely be reopened, in birds or in people, is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the Cold Face Test, a pulse count was 22 beats in 15 seconds at rest. It was 18 beats in 15 seconds with the face in cold water. How many beats a minute is each count? By how many beats a minute did the heart slow?
maths.answer: 88 beats a minute at rest and 72 beats a minute with the face in cold water. The heart slowed by 16 beats a minute.
maths.explain: One minute is four lots of 15 seconds. 22 times 4 is 88. 18 times 4 is 72. 88 minus 72 is 16.
maths.context: In the Cold Face Test you hold your breath with your face in cold water. A grown-up counts your pulse for 15 seconds. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: Doctors and scientists give heartbeats as beats a minute. Multiplying by 4 turns a short count into that unit, so that your result can be compared with others.

maths.problem: Three pulse counts for one test in the Cold Face Test were 18, 17 and 24. One of them is probably a miscount. Which count best describes the test: the middle one, or the biggest one? Why?
maths.answer: The middle count, 18. The count of 24 is far from the other two and is probably a mistake.
maths.explain: In order, the counts are 17, 18 and 24. Two of the three agree closely. The middle count stays sensible even when one count is far off.
maths.context: In the Cold Face Test each test is done three times, and you circle the middle count of the three. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: A middle value is not pulled about by one wrong count. That is why the Cold Face Test uses it.

maths.problem: A seal's heart beats about 100 times a minute at the surface. On a dive it beats about 10 times a minute. How many beats does her heart make in a 15-minute dive? How many would it have made at the surface rate?
maths.answer: 150 beats during the dive. At the surface rate it would have been 1,500 beats, which is 1,350 more.
maths.explain: 10 times 15 is 150. 100 times 15 is 1,500. 1,500 minus 150 is 1,350. Every beat uses oxygen, so far fewer beats means the oxygen lasts longer.
maths.context: In the Cold Face Test your heart slowed a little with your face in cold water. A seal has the same diving reflex, and hers is much stronger.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how much work the seal's heart is spared on one dive. This explains what the reflex is for.

maths.problem: In the Big Eyes Test, 8 voters chose between two faces. If eye size made no difference, about how many votes would the big-eyed face get? Is 7 out of 8 strong evidence that eye size matters? Is 5 out of 8?
maths.answer: About 4 votes if eye size made no difference. 7 out of 8 is strong evidence. 5 out of 8 is weak evidence.
maths.explain: With two faces and no real preference, each face gets about half of the votes. Half of 8 is 4. A score of 7 is far from 4. A score of 5 is only one vote away from 4, which can easily happen by chance.
maths.context: In the Big Eyes Test you show people two drawn faces that differ only in eye size. You ask which face is cuter. These are made-up votes.
maths.why_maths: Knowing what chance alone would give tells you whether your votes mean anything.

maths.problem: On the ducklings' graph, 3 ducklings out of 10 imprinted at 1 to 4 hours. At 13 to 16 hours, 9 out of 10 imprinted. At 29 to 32 hours, none did. A duckling first meets a moving thing at 45 hours. Predict what happens, and say how the pattern tells you.
maths.answer: She will almost certainly not imprint on it.
maths.explain: The numbers rise to a peak at 13 to 16 hours. Then they fall to 0 by 29 to 32 hours. Past that age the line stays at 0, and 45 hours is well past it.
maths.context: In When Does the Window Close you draw a line graph of how many ducklings imprint at each age. The numbers are made up but follow a real pattern.
maths.why_maths: A line graph shows where the peak is and where the line reaches zero. From that shape you can predict an age that was never tested.

maths.problem: In the Yawn Spread, 3 of 6 volunteers yawned after seeing yawns. On the day of smiles, 1 of the same 6 yawned. Write each result as a fraction. Which is bigger, and what does the difference suggest?
maths.answer: Three sixths, which is one half, after yawns. One sixth after smiles. One half is bigger, which suggests that seeing a yawn sets off yawns.
maths.explain: 3 out of 6 is the same as 1 out of 2. 1 out of 6 is smaller than 3 out of 6. With only 6 volunteers this is a hint, and more volunteers would make it stronger.
maths.context: In the Yawn Spread you yawn in front of six people on one day. You smile in front of them on the next. Each day you count who yawns. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Fractions let you compare the two days fairly, and show how big the difference is.

warmup.a: A fast, automatic response of the body to one stimulus, which nobody has to learn.

warmup.q: Name the stimulus and the response when a sock ball flies at your face.
warmup.a: The stimulus is something rushing at the eyes. The response is a blink.

warmup.q: What does your heart do when your face is in cold water and you hold your breath?
warmup.a: It beats more slowly. This is the diving reflex.

warmup.q: What is a fixed action pattern?
warmup.a: A set of inborn movements in a set order, which usually runs to the end once started.

warmup.q: What is a sign stimulus? Give one example.
warmup.a: The one feature that sets off an inborn behaviour, such as the red spot on a gull's beak.
Fast learning in a short time early in life, such as a gosling learning whom to follow.
The short time when a kind of learning, such as imprinting, can happen.

warmup.q: What is a supernormal stimulus? Give one example.
warmup.a: A made-up trigger that works better than the real one. A giant egg and a cartoon face with huge eyes are examples.

quiz: A reflex has to be learned by practice.
A reflex is inborn. Your blink and your knee kick worked without any lessons.
Cold water on the face, with the breath held, slows a person's heart.
This is the diving reflex, which humans share with seals and ducks.
A goose stops rolling at once if her egg is taken away halfway.
She finishes the movement. A fixed action pattern usually runs to the end.
A gosling is born knowing what her mother looks like.
She is born with the urge to follow. She learns whom to follow by imprinting.
Imprinting can happen only during a short time after hatching.
This time is the sensitive period. For mallard ducklings this is about the first day.
A koel raised by crows still calls like a koel.
The koel's call is innate. Every koel is raised by foster birds.
A gull chick pecks at the red spot on a parent's beak.
The red spot is the sign stimulus that sets off pecking.
An oystercatcher always chooses her own egg over a giant egg.
She chooses the giant egg. It is a supernormal stimulus.
You can stop a swallow halfway if you try hard.
Once a swallow starts, the muscles work in a set order to the end.
Animals who have instincts can also learn.
Instinct gives a start, and learning improves on it. A bird's second nest is better than her first.
odd: The blink, the knee kick and mouth-watering are reflexes, but cycling is learned.
The egg, the stick and the cartoon are supernormal stimuli, but a real beak is the normal one.
Ducklings, goslings and hen chicks walk and imprint soon after hatching, but a sparrow chick stays in the nest.
Seals, ducks and humans have the diving reflex, but an earthworm has no lungs or face to cool.
Egg rolling, nut burying and swallowing are fixed action patterns, but a song is learned by practice.

how_we_found_out.story: For centuries people thought a chick or a gosling was born knowing their own mother. In 1873 Douglas Spalding, a largely self-taught scientist who grew up in Scotland, tested this. He put small hoods over the eyes of chicks as they hatched. He took the hoods off a day or two later. The chicks followed him, the first moving thing they saw. Chicks unhooded after four days ran away from him instead. Spalding died young, and his work was forgotten. In Berlin, Oskar and Magdalena Heinroth raised hundreds of kinds of birds by hand in their flat. In 1911 Oskar wrote that new goslings took the first person they saw as their parent. Konrad Lorenz, in Austria, made the test that people remember. In 1935 he reported splitting a clutch of greylag goose eggs. The goose hatched half, and he hatched half. Her goslings followed her. His goslings followed him, even after the two groups were mixed. He named this imprinting. In 1973 he shared a Nobel Prize with Niko Tinbergen and Karl von Frisch. Lorenz had also joined the Nazi party in 1938 and written in support of its ideas about race. He later said that he regretted this.
how_we_found_out.who: Douglas Spalding in Britain, Oskar and Magdalena Heinroth in Germany, and Konrad Lorenz in Austria. Niko Tinbergen worked with Lorenz on fixed action patterns.
how_we_found_out.when: Spalding published in 1873, Oskar Heinroth in 1911 and Lorenz in 1935. Lorenz, Tinbergen and Karl von Frisch shared the Nobel Prize in 1973.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a young bird is born knowing their own mother. Spalding's chicks and Lorenz's goslings followed a man instead, because he was the first moving thing they saw. The urge to follow is inborn, but whom to follow is learned.
