roots.context: In the Cold Face Test, cold water on your face slowed your heart. You also met ducklings who are born ready to follow. Here we ask where know-how comes from when nobody taught it.

deep_truth.truth: In the Cold Face Test, cool water on your face slowed your heart. Seals, dolphins and ducks have the same reflex, and it saves their air on a dive. Scientists think we all inherited it from shared ancestors, who lived long before there were humans. So some of what your body knows how to do is older than humankind.
deep_truth.habit: We think of what we know as what we learned in our own lifetime. A reflex is know-how that was ready before our first lesson, and it reached us from ancestors.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Cold Face Test the pulse count usually falls by 2 to 5 beats with a cold, wet face. Nobody practised that. The same slowing was measured in ducks by Paul Bert in 1870 and in seals by Per Scholander in 1940.

three.who_am_i: You are someone who learns new things. But you also carry abilities that are much older than you. Your blink, your swallow and your slowing heart were ready before your first lesson.
three.what_is_life: Every living being begins with abilities that were handed down from their parents, and then adds what they learn themselves. A duckling is given the urge to follow, and finds out for herself whom to follow.
three.what_is_this_world: A body is not finished without the world around it. A reflex needs something to set it off, such as cold water on the face. A duckling's urge to follow needs something to follow, such as a moving mother.

roots.thread: The diving reflex is in the seal, the duck, the dolphin and you. These are separate bodies, and they carry the same piece of know-how, because they grew from the same ancestors. A gosling is handed the urge to follow, and the world around her supplies the rest. The Upanishads teach that one life looks out through many bodies. Biology does not say that, but it says something close. All animals are one family, and much of what each one can do was inherited from that family.

teachings.source: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 2.9, with the old commentary of Vyasa
teachings.teaching: The sutra says that the will to go on living flows by itself, even in the wise. Vyasa adds that even a newborn worm shrinks from danger, though nothing in this life has taught them to.
teachings.link: These thinkers noticed what this unit tests: a newborn animal acts rightly with no lesson. They explained it by earlier lives of the same being. Biology explains it by the lives of ancestors, passed on through DNA. The two answers differ, but the question is the same.

teachings.teaching: Mencius says that anyone who sees a small child about to fall into a well feels alarm at once. They feel alarm and pity before any thought of praise or reward.
teachings.link: Mencius was arguing that goodness starts from something inborn, and he was not doing biology. Yet he describes a response in every person that one particular sight sets off. Lorenz's idea about baby faces is a later version of the same thought.

teachings.teaching: The verse says that even a wise person acts according to their own nature. All beings follow their nature, and forcing alone achieves little.
teachings.link: In Find the Trigger you knew the sock ball could not hit you, and you blinked anyway. The next verse of the Gita adds that a person need not be ruled by every pull. Humans can notice an urge and still choose what to do after it.

science.text: All animals with backbones share ancestors and inherit their bodies through DNA. The diving reflex has been found in every air-breathing kind that has been tested.
In 1890 William James argued that humans have more instincts than other animals, not fewer. Scientists still argue about how much of what people do starts from instinct.

other_view.who: Zing-Yang Kuo, a Chinese psychologist, from 1921
other_view.view: Kuo argued that the word instinct explains nothing. He raised kittens together with rats, and most of those cats never killed a rat. On his view, each behaviour is built up step by step from the first days of the embryo. What we call inherited know-how is growth that nobody has traced yet.

practice.title: The breath that needs no planning
practice.say: Sit still together and close your eyes. Breathe out slowly, and then wait without breathing in. Notice the moment when your body starts the next breath by itself. Do this three times. Then breathe as usual for one minute, and notice each breath arrive without any plan from you.
practice.kid: Sit still. Breathe out and wait. Feel your body start the next breath. Did you plan that breath?

ask: In the Cold Face Test your heart slowed, and you did not plan it. Who or what knew how to do that?
A duckling is born ready to learn one thing in her first day. What do you think you were born ready to learn?
If part of your know-how is older than humankind, where does 'you' begin?

playtest: Read through step by step as a parent and child in a city flat would use it. Not yet done at home. The Cold Face Test (core) needs a wide bowl, cold water, a towel and a timer. A grown-up stays beside the child the whole time. The water must be as cold as fridge water. In water from the tap in an Indian summer the pulse hardly changes. Expect the face-in-water count to be 2 to 5 beats lower in 15 seconds. A beat or two of counting error is normal. That is why each test is done three times and the middle count is used. Some children show little change, and the steps say to record what really happens. The wet towel method is gentler and gives a smaller change. Leave the test out if the child has a cold, an ear infection, breathing trouble or a heart condition. Find the Trigger needs a clear plastic folder or a closed glass window. It also needs a rolled sock, a blunt pencil and a lemon. A ticklish child may pull the foot away before the toes curl, and that is fine. The Swallow Test needs only water, with small sips. The Big Eyes Test needs four paper cards, a tumbler, a 1-rupee coin and at least 8 voters. They can be asked in person, over a day, or by sending a photo of each pair. The big-eyed face and the low-eyed face usually win clearly. With 8 voters a close result is possible, and the step says to ask more people. The ducklings' graph uses made-up numbers that follow the shape of Eckhard Hess's results, and the activity says so. The Yawn Spread depends on who is tired, so its result varies from family to family. The Crane Puppet works with a sock and clothes pegs. No part needs a garden, a pet or a wild animal. Facts to treat with care: Tinbergen's stickleback result is marked as debated. The seal's heart rate of about 100 falling to about 10 is a rounded figure from Scholander's seals. Lorenz's test with a split clutch is told as he reported it. The story of the chappals is imagined, and fits what is known about imprinting. The Yoga Sutra, Mencius and Gita passages are given as paraphrases. The three videos have no address yet.
